```{r load}
library(bbssr)
```

## Design and notation

In a matched-pairs design both treatments are applied to the same unit, as in a cross-over trial, a comparison of two diagnostic procedures on the same patients, or a trial that treats one eye of each patient with each treatment. A pair has one of four outcomes. Let $p_{10}$ be the probability that only treatment 1 responds and $p_{01}$ the probability that only treatment 2 responds. The difference of the response probabilities of the two treatments is $\delta = p_{10} - p_{01}$, and the probability of a discordant pair is $\psi = p_{10} + p_{01}$. Among $N$ pairs, let $a$ and $b$ be the numbers of the two kinds of discordant pairs. All tests of the package depend on the data only through $(a, b)$.

The `Paired*` functions follow the `Binary*` functions for two independent groups: `PairedRR()`, `PairedPower()` and `PairedSampleSize()` for the fixed design, and `PairedPowerBSSR()`, `PairedBSSR()`, `PairedTypeIErrorBSSR()` and `PairedAlphaAdjBSSR()` for blinded sample size re-estimation.

## Tests

Six tests are available. `'McNemar'` refers $Z = (a - b) / \sqrt{a + b}$ to the standard normal distribution, and `'McNemar-cc'` refers $(|a - b| - 1) / \sqrt{a + b}$ to it, with the continuity correction of formula (2) of Fagerland et al. (2013), and $(a - b - 1) / \sqrt{a + b}$ for the alternative `'greater'` and $(b - a - 1) / \sqrt{a + b}$ for `'less'`. `'McNemar-exact'` refers $a$ to the binomial distribution with $a + b$ trials and probability 1/2, and `'McNemar-midP'` is its mid-p version (Fagerland et al., 2013). `'McNemar-uncond'` orders the outcomes by $Z$ and maximizes the null tail probability over $\psi$ (Suissa and Shuster, 1991; Berger and Sidik, 2003), optionally with the Berger-Boos procedure. `'Paired-Score'` is the score test of Nam (1997) and Tango (1998) for the null hypothesis $\delta = -\text{margin}$, which reduces to `'McNemar'` with a margin of 0.

The example of Berger and Sidik (2003, Section 4) has $n = 30$ pairs with $x_{10} = 11$ and $x_{01} = 4$ and tests $p_{10} \le p_{01}$ against $p_{10} > p_{01}$.

```{r berger-sidik}
pv <- function(...) attr(PairedRR(N = 30, alpha = 0.05, ...), 'p.value')[12, 5]
p.bs <- c(exact = pv(Test = 'McNemar-exact'),
          asymptotic = pv(Test = 'McNemar'),
          unconditional = pv(Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE),
          berger.boos = pv(Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE, bb.gamma = 0.0005))
round(p.bs, 4)
```

The p-values `r paste(sprintf('%.4f', p.bs), collapse = ', ')` are those of the tests CB, M, Z and $Z_C$ in Table 3 of Berger and Sidik (2003). The rejection region of a test is a triangle of possible outcomes.

```{r rr-plot}
plot(PairedRR(N = 30, alpha = 0.05, Test = 'McNemar-uncond', ref.pvalue = TRUE))
```

## Power and number of pairs

The power is the probability of the rejection region under the multinomial distribution of $(a, b, N - a - b)$, computed by enumeration. The normal approximation to the number of pairs is formula (9) of Nam (1997), which is formula (3) of Connor (1987) when the margin is 0. In the example of Connor (1987, p. 210) the response probabilities are 0.8 and 0.7 and $\psi = 0.3$, so $p_{10} = 0.2$ and $p_{01} = 0.1$.

```{r connor}
n.std <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                          Test = 'McNemar', method = 'standard')
n.exact <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                            Test = 'McNemar-exact')
n.midp <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.2, p01 = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.9,
                           Test = 'McNemar-midP')
c(standard = n.std$N, exact = n.exact$N, midp = n.midp$N)
```

The normal approximation gives `r n.std$N` pairs, as in Connor (1987). The exact search needs `r n.exact$N` pairs for the exact conditional test and `r n.midp$N` for its mid-p version.

## Blinded sample size re-estimation

The number of discordant pairs can be counted without unblinding: a pair is discordant whatever treatment responded. At an interim analysis after $n_{1}$ pairs, the blinded estimate of $\psi$ is $D_{1} / n_{1}$, where $D_{1}$ is the number of discordant pairs. The assumed difference `Delta.A` is kept, and the estimate is raised to $|\Delta_{A}|$ when it is smaller. The number of pairs is then re-estimated by the normal approximation (`ss.method = 'standard'`), by the exact search (`'exact'`), or by the smallest number at which the conditional power given $D_{1}$ reaches the target (`'conditional.power'`), the rule of Schepers et al. (2026). The re-estimation depends on the data only through $D_{1}$, and given the numbers of discordant pairs the direction of each discordant pair is independent of them, so the power is computed exactly.

Schepers et al. (2026) plan the exact conditional test at the two-sided level 0.05 with $\Delta_{A} = 0.15$ and $\psi = 0.2$.

```{r plan}
plan <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.175, p01 = 0.025, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                         Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
                         search = 'smallest')
plan$N
```

```{r bssr}
res <- PairedPowerBSSR(psi = c(0.15, 0.2, 0.3), Delta.T = 0.15, Delta.A = 0.15,
                       N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
                       ss.method = 'conditional.power', N.max = 200)
res
```

With $\psi = 0.3$ the fixed design of `r plan$N` pairs has power `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.TRAD[3])`, and the re-estimation design `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.BSSR[3])` with `r sprintf('%.1f', res$E.N[3])` pairs on average. With $\psi = 0.15$ the fixed design has power `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.TRAD[1])` and the re-estimation design `r sprintf('%.3f', res$power.BSSR[1])`.

`PairedBSSR()` performs the re-estimation of a single trial. With 5 discordant pairs among 30 interim pairs:

```{r single}
PairedBSSR(n1 = 30, D1 = 5, Delta.A = 0.15, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
           Test = 'McNemar-exact', alternative = 'two.sided',
           ss.method = 'conditional.power', N.max = 200)
```

## Type I error rate

The exact conditional test keeps its level after any blinded re-estimation, since the number of pairs in which only treatment 1 responds stays binomial given the total number of discordant pairs (Schepers et al., 2026). The other tests have a type I error rate that depends on $\psi$, and the re-estimation can change it. `PairedTypeIErrorBSSR()` computes the rate on the boundary $p_{10} = p_{01}$ and certifies its largest value. In the example the final number of pairs is at most 150.

```{r tie}
tie <- PairedTypeIErrorBSSR(Delta.A = 0.15, N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.025,
                            tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'McNemar', ss.method = 'standard',
                            N.max = 150)
attr(tie, 'max')
plot(tie)
```

The largest type I error rate of the asymptotic McNemar test at the one-sided level 0.025 is `r sprintf('%.4f', attr(tie, 'max')$TIE[1])` for the re-estimation design and `r sprintf('%.4f', attr(tie, 'max')$TIE[2])` for the fixed design. `PairedAlphaAdjBSSR()` lowers the nominal level until the rate is controlled.

```{r adj}
adj <- PairedAlphaAdjBSSR(Delta.A = 0.15, N = plan$N, n.interim = 30, alpha = 0.025,
                          tar.power = 0.8, Test = 'McNemar', ss.method = 'standard',
                          N.max = 150)
adj
```

## Non-inferiority and equivalence

The score test takes a margin. With `alternative = 'greater'` and `margin = 0.05` it tests $\delta \le -0.05$ against $\delta > -0.05$. Nam (1997, Section 5) plans a trial with $p_{01} = 0.05$, $\delta_{0} = -0.05$ and $\delta_{1} = 0$ at the one-sided level 0.05 with power 0.8.

```{r nam}
ni <- PairedSampleSize(p10 = 0.05, p01 = 0.05, alpha = 0.05, tar.power = 0.8,
                       Test = 'Paired-Score', margin = 0.05)
c(normal = attr(ni, 'n.raw'), exact = ni$N)
```

Formula (9) of Nam (1997) gives `r sprintf('%.1f', attr(ni, 'n.raw'))` pairs, and the exact power of the score test reaches 0.8 with `r ni$N` pairs. With `alternative = 'equivalence'` and `margin = c(lower, upper)` the null hypothesis $\delta \le -\text{lower}$ or $\delta \ge \text{upper}$ is tested by two one-sided score tests. In a re-estimation design the type I error rate is evaluated on both boundaries.

## References

Berger, R. L. and Sidik, K. (2003). Exact unconditional tests for a 2 &times; 2 matched-pairs design. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research*, 12, 91-108.

Connor, R. J. (1987). Sample size for testing differences in proportions for the paired-sample design. *Biometrics*, 43, 207-211.

Fagerland, M. W., Lydersen, S. and Laake, P. (2013). The McNemar test for binary matched-pairs data: mid-p and asymptotic are better than exact conditional. *BMC Medical Research Methodology*, 13, 91.

Nam, J. (1997). Establishing equivalence of two treatments and sample size requirements in matched-pairs design. *Biometrics*, 53, 1422-1430.

Schepers, M., Brannath, W., Hoffmann, E., Stingl, J. and Schmidtmann, I. (2026). Blinded sample size review for McNemar's test based on primary and surrogate endpoints. arXiv:2608.17784.

Suissa, S. and Shuster, J. J. (1991). The 2 x 2 matched-pairs trial: exact unconditional design and analysis. *Biometrics*, 47, 361-372.

Tango, T. (1998). Equivalence test and confidence interval for the difference in proportions for the paired-sample design. *Statistics in Medicine*, 17, 891-908.
